doc.title: Melba Liston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Back to Dizzy in New York and the audience's reaction
summary: Dizzy sent for her again about 1949; the musicians were cool but audiences were surprised at a woman trombonist, and Wilson had introduced her as a complete musician.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: No, I wasn’t unhappy. I just – one day I said no. I quit that. Just me and music again. Then maybe Dizzy sent for me again.
I went back to New York to stay.
But what kind of greeting did you get? You took music, right?
Yeah. The guys were cool, but the audience, said, “Girl, (murmur murmur).”
Nobody had played no trombone. Nobody.
Yeah. You broke the ice. You were the innovator.
Gerald, he started it. “She wrote the arrangement. She plays, she sings, and all of that stuff.”
He did? He told Dizzy that?
No. He would do that when we were working. Dizzy was the same. He followed up the same way. But the guys were cool.
